Louis Lumière. French inventor and filmmaker, along with his brother Auguste, who pioneered cinematography and the motion-picture camera, creating some of cinema's first narrative films—brief, observed moments of everyday life. Though not filmmakers in the narrative sense, their technological and aesthetic innovations established cinema as a viable medium for capturing life and distributing images worldwide.

They invented the Cinématographe, a portable camera-and-projector combined, superior to Edison's Kinetoscope in portability and commercial viability. Louis filmed L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat in 1896, a fifty-second shot of a train approaching the camera. Legend holds that audiences were startled by the approaching locomotive. He produced La Sortie de l'Usine Lumière à Lyon in 1894, a minute-long film showing workers and bicycles leaving their father's factory—among the first narrative footage.

The Lumière brothers dispatched camera operators around the world to film local scenes, creating the first global cinema distribution network and archiving life across the globe. They never pursued narrative cinema themselves. Their films remained documentary actualities, brief observed moments, privileging camera placement and light over storytelling. Their thousands of films create a visual archive of the eighteen-nineties—street scenes, colonial expeditions, family moments—a priceless anthropological record.

They established cinema as a commercial medium and international art. Though surpassed by narrative innovators, they remain foundational to cinema history. Georges Méliès was a contemporary who transformed the Lumières' documentary impulse into narrative fantasy. They are cinema's inventors. Thomas Edison was a rival inventor of the Kinetoscope, though Lumière's superior technology prevailed. They established the observational mode of documentary cinema.
